crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data covers the gathering of greenhouse gas figures across Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3, from fuel bills and meter readings through to supplier reports and spend records. It sits inside sustainability and carbon accounting, where the output feeds disclosure regimes, internal targets and audit. The work spans facilities, fleets, purchased energy and long supply chains, and it usually involves several departments rather than one team.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack is typically an emissions management platform or a spreadsheet model fed by utility portals, fuel card systems, ERP extracts and supplier questionnaires. Enterprise resource planning systems hold spend and procurement records that are often the practical starting point for Scope 3 estimates. Cloud storage and a governed data warehouse keep the underlying activity data traceable, and API connections increasingly replace manual downloads from utility and travel systems.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners map emission sources to an organisational boundary, choose a calculation method per source, and apply published emission factors to activity data. Spend based estimates are common where supplier specific data is missing, and they are later replaced as better data arrives. Quality checks, version control and a clear audit trail matter as much as the arithmetic, because the same figure may be restated across reporting years.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on data ownership, supplier confidentiality and the accuracy of what is published. Assurance providers expect documented methods, source evidence and a named owner for each data set, and voluntary frameworks plus mandatory disclosure rules shape what must be reported. Estimates carry restatement risk, and supplier data may be shared under restrictions that limit how it can be reused or disclosed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more supplier specific data, tighter assurance and greater use of machine learning to classify spend, detect anomalies and fill gaps in activity records. Regulatory reporting requirements continue to expand, which pushes organisations toward continuous collection rather than annual exercises. The open questions are how quickly estimated figures can be replaced with measured ones and how far automated collection can be trusted without human review.
